big: A momentum index fund gained 40% last year. Index funds are meant to be dull, so how can one be a star? It follows a rule about which shares to hold. Rules have good years and bad years.

lines: This momentum index fund gave 40% last year. Should I switch everything into it?
Let us see what a rule-based index does over a full decade first, and how much of your money should ever ride on one.

alt: Three bars of share weights: by market size, by calm movement and by recent gains
caps: A plain index gives most weight to the biggest companies. Here four made-up shares, A to D.
A low volatility index gives most weight to the shares that swing the least.
A momentum index leans towards shares that rose the most lately. Weights are examples.
Each fund simply follows its rule. The fund is passive, but choosing the rule was an active choice.

alt: Three lines for a market index, a momentum index and a low volatility index over ten years with the deepest fall of each
caps: Made-up paths. Momentum leads for three years, gaining 25%, 30% and then 40%.
Then it turns. It falls 32% in one year and lags for years after.
Low volatility is steadier, but never the star. The plain index sits between.
Deepest falls: market -8%, momentum -40%, low volatility -2%. The best year does not repeat on demand.

alt: Bars comparing the loss on ten lakh rupees when half or a tenth of it is in a factor fund that falls 40 percent
caps: Say the factor fund falls 40%, as momentum did here, and the rest of the portfolio stays flat.
With half the money in it, the portfolio loses 20%, which is ₹2 lakh on ₹10 lakh.
With a tenth of the money in it, the portfolio loses 4%, which is ₹40,000.
A small satellite lets you hold an idea without letting it decide your future.

q: After a 40% year, Rohan puts ₹5 lakh into a momentum index fund. In the next two made-up years it falls 32% and then 12%. About what is his money worth?
opts: About ₹2.8 lakh, as 32% plus 12% is a 44% fall
About ₹3.4 lakh, as only the 32% fall really counts
About ₹3.0 lakh, as each fall hits the reduced sum
About ₹4.4 lakh, as the fund still shows a 3-year gain
why: Adding the falls gives 44%, which would leave ₹2.8 lakh. A second fall acts on the reduced amount, so this is too low.
₹3.4 lakh is where the money stands after the 32% fall alone. The next 12% fall takes it lower.
₹5 lakh times 0.68 times 0.88 is about ₹2.99 lakh. The second fall applies to the smaller sum.
The 40% gain came before he invested. Only the two falls count for his ₹5 lakh, so ₹4.4 lakh is far too high.

q: Meena asks what makes a momentum index fund "smart beta". Which description is accurate?
opts: An active fund where a manager picks shares with good news
A plain index fund under a new name, with the same holdings
A fund that guarantees to beat the market using past winners
Passive in how it runs, active in which rule it follows
why: No manager picks shares each day. The fund follows the rule's index, and that is what makes it passive.
A plain index follows market size. A rule-based index holds different shares in different weights.
A rule based on past winners cannot promise future results. Momentum can reverse sharply.
The fund mechanically copies a rule-based index, but someone chose the rule, so an active decision sits behind it.

q: Rohan is excited about a factor fund and wants half of his ₹10 lakh portfolio in it. If it fell 40% and the rest stayed flat, he would lose ₹2 lakh. What should the adviser suggest?
opts: Half is fine, since factor funds recover from every fall quickly
A small satellite slice, so a bad year cannot sink the plan
Skip all equity, since a factor fund shows equity is too risky
Put it all in, since a bigger bet earns more if the rule works
why: A factor can lag for years after a fall. Recovery is not quick or sure, so half is too large.
With about a tenth in it, the same fall costs 4% of the portfolio, or ₹40,000. He keeps the idea without staking his plan.
One factor fund does not make all equity unsuitable. The answer is to size it small, not to avoid equity.
A bigger bet also loses more when the rule fails. Factors go through long cycles, and all-in is the worst-case size.

q: A new factor fund has a two-year record, charges 0.8% a year, and a plain Nifty index fund charges 0.2%. What should Meena do before buying?
opts: Buy it, since a fee 0.6% higher shows that it is run better
Skip the check, as a rule-based fund tracks the market anyway
Learn the rule, accept possible lag, use a small slice
Wait for its best one-year return, then invest a large amount
why: Fee does not measure quality. A higher cost only means a higher hurdle for the rule to beat the plain index.
A rule-based fund can swing far from the market, as momentum did in the film, so a check is needed.
Factors have long cycles. A short record and a higher cost mean she should know the rule and keep the slice small.
Buying after the best year is chasing. Momentum reverses fast, so that is when the risk is highest.

pts: Smart beta follows an index built on a rule, such as low volatility or momentum.
Factors go through long cycles. A star year can be followed by years of lag.
Costs are higher and records short. Use a small satellite, and know the rule first.
